title: Is Teaching a Science or a Craft?
author: Paul Kirschner and Nidhi Sachdeva
summary: Paul Kirschner and Nidhi Sachdeva take on the long-running debate over whether teaching is a science or a craft and call it a false dichotomy. They first dismantle the myth that great teachers are born with a knack, noting that the myth conveniently excuses teacher education, districts and governments from the work of developing teachers systematically. The science of teaching is described as five building blocks drawn from their book Becoming an Expert Teacher: subject knowledge, cognitive and educational psychology, instructional techniques, instructional tools and pedagogy. Craft is the practical wisdom that emerges when that knowledge is enacted, adapted and refined in real classrooms. The authors argue that initial teacher education should teach the science explicitly, while craft is cultivated over time through induction, mentoring, reflection and guided experience. They warn that without science teaching drifts toward myths and eminence-based fads, and without craft it becomes rigid and mechanical.
points: Treating teaching as a natural knack excuses institutions from the systematic work of preparing and supporting teachers.
The science of teaching rests on five building blocks: subject knowledge, how we learn, how we teach, what we use and how we relate.
Craft is not vague intuition but scientific knowledge in action, shown in judgments about when to slow down, press on, model again or let silence work.
Initial teacher education suits the explicit teaching of science, whereas craft grows through structured induction, mentoring, feedback and reflection.
Induction that offers only emotional support helps a beginner survive but not grow, so novices need something closer to a medical residency.
quotes: It’s one of those arguments that sounds important until you realise it’s actually a false dichotomy. Teaching isn’t one or the other; it’s both.

Also, calling teaching a knack trivialises it while at the same time conveniently excusing schools of education, school districts, and governments from the hard work of systematically developing and supporting it.
Cognitive psychology matters because teaching that ignores how people learn is always going to be weaker than teaching that works with human cognition rather than against it.
This is where things get interesting, because craft is not the opposite of science. It’s what happens when scientific knowledge is enacted, adapted, and refined in real classrooms.
Craft is not vague intuition. It’s knowledge (the scientific knowledge) in action; wisdom.
Put simply, the science can be (and should be) taught quite explicitly at the outset; the craft has to be cultivated and developed through guided experience.
If we assume teaching is mainly craft, we risk underpreparing teachers scientifically and leaving them to pick things up by trial and error or use their gut feelings/common (non)sense.
Without craft, teaching can become rigid, mechanical, and oddly inhuman, as though knowing the research were enough to tell us what to do in the classroom.
